title: Guha the boatman
hook: a boat on the Ganga, Sita's prayer in midstream, and a famous boatman who isn't in Valmiki

segments.voice: Yesterday: Guha the boatman, part two. A night watch by the fire, matted hair at dawn, and Sumantra sent home. Did you listen to someone and stay? Today, across the river. Day five hundred thirty-six.

If you've heard this part of the story in a temple or at a family reading, you may remember a boatman who won't let Rama into his boat until he's washed his feet. He's afraid, he says with a grin, that the dust of those feet will turn his wooden boat into a woman, the way it once turned a stone into Ahalya. It's a lovely, funny scene. It comes from a later retelling, Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas. Valmiki's crossing is simpler, and it has its own quiet center.
screen: `WASH YOUR FEET FIRST.` → `A STORY FROM TULSIDAS.` → `VALMIKI'S CROSSING IS SIMPLER.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki, it's Guha who arranges everything. He has a strong, well-made boat brought down to the bank, with oarsmen ready. Rama thanks him and says goodbye. Sita steps in first, then Lakshmana, then Rama, and the oarsmen push off into the current. In the middle of the river, Sita does something worth noticing. She folds her hands and speaks to the river itself, to Ganga, as a goddess. She asks Ganga to protect Rama through the fourteen years and bring the three of them back safely. And she makes a vow: when they return, she will worship the river with offerings. It's not a prayer we'll repeat here, but its shape matters. The first time the exiles leave dry land, Sita turns the crossing into worship. In Hindu tradition, the Ganga is still this: a goddess and a mother as well as a river, someone you can speak to. The boat reaches the far bank. Now they're truly outside the kingdom. Rama sets an order for walking. Lakshmana goes first, to clear the way. Sita walks in the middle. Rama walks last, guarding them both. Guha watches them from the far shore until they're gone among the trees. So Valmiki's boatman isn't the comic figure of the later story. He's a king, a friend, a host who keeps watch all night and provides the boat. Two retellings, two boatmen. Valmiki's is the one who stays on the bank, watching.
screen: `GUHA BRINGS A STRONG BOAT.` · `SITA SPEAKS TO THE RIVER.` · `THE GANGA, GODDESS AND MOTHER.` · `LAKSHMANA AHEAD, RAMA BEHIND.` · then, large: `GUHA WATCHES FROM THE SHORE.`

segments.voice: Sit and imagine you're in a small boat in the middle of a wide river. Feel the gentle rocking. Breathe in as the boat rises a little, breathe out as it settles. You're between two shores: what you're leaving, and what's ahead. Don't hurry toward either. Just ride the breath in the middle of the river. If you pray, you can ask for safe passage, in your own way. The bell holds the time.
Guha the boatman, part three. He sees the exiles across the Ganga, Sita prays to the river in midstream, and Guha watches them disappear into the forest.
Your line: Guha the boatman. Today, when you cross from one part of your day to the next, pause for a breath in the middle. Day five hundred thirty-six.

howItsDone: Hindu pilgrims bathe in the Ganga, offer lamps and flowers to it, and speak to it as Ganga Ma, a mother goddess; in the text, Sita prays to the river in midstream.

fork.setup: you're Sita, in a boat in the middle of the Ganga, at the start of fourteen years of exile. what do you do?
options: fold your hands and speak to the river.
ask the oarsmen to turn back.
fork.reveal: she prays to Ganga to protect them and bring them home, and vows offerings on their return.

original.note: Sanskrit gaṅgā: the river Ganga, honored as a goddess and a mother; the river the exiles cross today.

trapdoor: what you thought: the boatman who ferried Rama is a humble ferryman.
what it means: in Valmiki, it's Guha, a king and Rama's friend, who provides the boat.
what a scholar hears: the foot-washing boatman, often called Kevat, comes from the Ramcharitmanas, one of the places where Tulsidas adds a devotional scene to Valmiki's frame.
